## 31. Workstream 4 — Decentralized Blockchain Access

### 31.1 Separate correctness from liveness, and the problem halves

The single most useful move in this workstream is a distinction the current
design already implies but never states:

```text
  CORRECTNESS  — "is this answer true?"       solved, by the light client
  LIVENESS     — "can I get an answer at all?" not solved, and it is the
                                                actual centralisation
```

`internal/ethproof` verifies sync-committee signatures and Merkle-Patricia
proofs, so a lying provider produces proofs that fail verification. **Correctness
is already trust-minimised and this workstream must not re-litigate it.** What
remains is that the PoF architecture routes every node's chain access through a
website-run External Node, paymaster and relayer, and the resolver needs a beacon
source and an RPC. Those are single points of *observation, censorship and
unavailability*, and none of them can be fixed by a better proof.

| Property | Status | Attack that remains |
|---|---|---|
| Provider cannot lie about state | **Solved** — `VerifyProof` against a light-client-verified `stateRoot` | None; a lie is a detectable failure |
| Provider cannot lie about absence | **Solved** — absence proofs terminate at the first divergent node (160 B, measured) | None |
| Provider cannot refuse | **Not solved** | Selective refusal, targeted at one node or one name |
| Provider cannot stall | **Not solved** | Freshness attack: serve only old-but-valid state |
| Provider cannot observe | **Not solved** | The relayer sees every registration; the RPC sees every query |
| Provider cannot be the only one | **Not solved** | Single External Node in the PoF design |
| Broadcast is verifiable | **Not solvable** — noted in `doc/ethereum-data-layer.md` §7 | A provider can accept a transaction and not broadcast it; only later inclusion is verifiable |

### 31.2 The mechanism: three sources, and chain evidence carried by AXON itself

**(a) `k_src` independent sources for liveness.** Correctness needs one source;
liveness needs several. Independence is defined structurally, not by count:
distinct operator, distinct ASN, and — where possible — distinct client
implementation. `k_src = 3` is the floor, and the existing
`SetAnchor → ErrAnchorNotIndependent` rule (which refuses an anchor sharing a
registrable domain with the RPC) is exactly the right shape and should be
generalised to the source set.

**(b) Chain evidence distributed over AXON's own DHT.** This is the structural
fix, and the arithmetic is already measured in `doc/ethereum-data-layer.md`:

```text
  sync-committee updates    ~7.6 MB / year     append-only, immutable
  verified headers          ~2.7 GB / year     append-only, immutable
  storage proofs            on demand          immutable, cacheable
```

All of it is content-addressed and never rewritten — precisely what the storage
layer is for, and the P12-3 plan already anticipated putting it there. A node
that has the header chain and the committee updates **needs no RPC to verify a
read it has a proof for**, and proofs themselves are cacheable objects. The
dependency collapses from "an RPC provider" to "any source of immutable
append-only data", which the overlay is.

**(c) The relayer made optional and non-observing.** The PoF meta-transaction
design (`registerWithSig`, owner recovered on-chain) is already correct in that
the relayer cannot name the owner. What it lacks is plurality and privacy:
several independent relayers discovered through the DHT, self-submission always
available as a fallback, and submission over a circuit so the relayer learns a
transaction but not its origin.

### 31.3 The seventeen fields

| Field | Content |
|---|---|
| **Threat model** | The RPC or relayer operator; an adversary who can block access to them; a network position that isolates a node from the chain; and Ethereum itself as a systemic dependency |
| **Current AXON weakness** | Liveness, observation and censorship all rest on single providers; the PoF architecture explicitly centralises node chain access in a website-run stack |
| **Security objective** | (a) No single source causes an incorrect answer — already met, re-verified. (b) No single source causes unavailability: `k_src ≥ 3` independent. (c) `S_max` declared per resolver mode and enforced. (d) Recovery from prolonged isolation is specified and tested |
| **Candidate mechanisms** | Multi-source proof-carrying reads; chain evidence in the DHT; DHT-discovered execution endpoints; rotating providers; quorum on *availability* rather than on truth; local cached verified state; checkpoint diversity from mutually independent origins; relayer plurality with self-submission fallback |
| **Mechanisms rejected** | **Quorum voting on state values** — `doc/trust-anchor.md` §5C already rules that N-of-M provider agreement "must not be described as verification", and it is right: agreement among providers is not evidence, and adopting it would weaken a property the system already has. **A single canonical AXON RPC** — the centralisation being removed. **Running a full execution node per AXON node** — `doc/p146-local-execution-node.md` measured this and concluded it does not fit the infrastructure |
| **Protocol changes** | A `ChainEvidence` record class in the DHT (headers, committee updates, proofs); endpoint discovery records; a source-independence policy object |
| **Cryptographic changes** | None. BLS, SSZ and MPT verification exist and are mainnet-exercised |
| **DHT changes** | Bulk append-only evidence storage — ~2.7 GB/year is a real load and its retention policy, sharding and pruning must be specified against the erasure-coding parameters |
| **Economic changes** | Evidence storage and relaying are services the accounting plane can pay for, which is a natural fit for §14 but must not become a requirement for correctness |
| **Implementation changes** | `blockchain/sources.go` (multi-source with independence policy), `blockchain/evidence.go` (DHT publication and retrieval), `blockchain/relayers.go`, and generalising `ErrAnchorNotIndependent` to the whole source set |
| **Simulation methodology** | Fault injection over source availability: single-source failure, correlated failure by ASN, targeted refusal for one name, freshness attack, and total isolation for 1 h / 1 d / 1 w |
| **Adversarial test methodology** | A hostile provider container that serves valid-but-stale state, that refuses selectively for one `nameHash`, and that colludes with a second source; plus a partition that isolates chain access while leaving the overlay intact — the combined P3/P4 case |
| **Metrics** | `k_src` achieved in practice; `S_max` distribution under fault; probability of undetected staleness; time to recovery after isolation; fraction of reads servable from DHT evidence with no RPC |
| **Milestones** | M4.1 source-independence policy and multi-source client. M4.2 chain evidence published to and retrieved from the DHT. M4.3 relayer plurality and self-submission. M4.4 freshness-attack detection. M4.5 isolation-recovery test. M4.6 the §31.5 dependency statement |
| **Exit criteria** | E4.1 A read completes correctly with any `k_src − 1` sources hostile or absent — falsified by a single-source dependency found in the code path. E4.2 A stale-but-valid source is detected within `S_max` and reported, not silently used. E4.3 A node with no RPC access at all completes a verified read from DHT-carried evidence. E4.4 Registration completes without the website relayer. E4.5 After one week of total chain isolation, a node recovers to a verified head, and the resolver's behaviour during isolation matches §13.6 exactly |
| **Residual risks** | Broadcast remains unverifiable. The weak-subjectivity checkpoint remains a subjective input, and checkpoint diversity reduces but does not remove it. Evidence in the DHT is only as available as the DHT, which couples P4 to P3 in both directions. Ethereum itself — §31.5 |
| **New attacks introduced** | **Evidence-store poisoning** — invalid headers offered as DHT objects, cheap to serve and cheap to reject, so it is a bandwidth-waste attack rather than a correctness one. **Endpoint-discovery manipulation** — an adversary that controls DHT records for endpoints steers a node to its own sources, which is the P3 attack wearing a P4 costume and is why the two share a phase. **Independence-policy gaming** — sources that appear independent by ASN and are not |

### 31.4 What this workstream does NOT establish

- That broadcast can be verified. It cannot, and the asymmetry belongs in the
  challenge budget, as `doc/ethereum-data-layer.md` already says.
- That the initial checkpoint can be made objective. Weak subjectivity is
  inherent.
- That DHT-carried evidence is cheaper than an RPC. It is more *independent*;
  at ~2.7 GB/year it is certainly not lighter, and the trade must be stated.
- That the PoF relayer's privacy leak is closed. Submitting over a circuit hides
  the origin from the relayer, not the fact of the registration from the chain.

### 31.5 Is Ethereum a hidden central dependency? Yes, and here is the bound

The honest answer, which the roadmap must not soften: **while namespace ownership
is settled on Ethereum, an Ethereum-level failure is an AXON namespace failure.**
No amount of light-client verification changes that; it makes the dependency
*honest*, not absent.

What is bounded, and how:

| Ethereum event | AXON consequence | Bound |
|---|---|---|
| Provider censors one node | None | `k_src ≥ 3` |
| All reachable providers refuse | Resolution degrades to SNAPSHOT mode | Bounded by `S_max`; names keep resolving, registrations stop |
| Chain halts / does not finalise | No ownership changes; existing bindings hold | Indefinite for reads; registration and transfer unavailable |
| Deep reorg past finality | A recently transferred name may flip | §13.6's reorg window; reads at finalised head only |
| Contentious fork | Two namespaces exist | Unresolvable technically; resolvers pin a chain, and this is the §12.0a fork right in a new costume |
| Gas price spike | Registration becomes unaffordable | A censorship outcome by price; noted in §23 P9 |
| Ethereum ceases | Ownership becomes unupdatable, and the last snapshot is the permanent record | Services remain reachable at Layer 1 (§11.9) — which is the entire reason Layer 1 is the guarantee |

The last row is the design's answer to its own worst case, and it is why §11's
three-layer model is load-bearing rather than decorative.

## 32. Workstream 5 — Traffic-Analysis Resistance

### 32.1 Two problems that must never be reported as one

| | Website fingerprinting (WF) | Flow correlation |
|---|---|---|
| Adversary position | **One** point — the client's link or its guard | **Both** ends |
| Question asked | "Which of a known set of destinations is this?" | "Are these two flows the same flow?" |
| Realistic defence | Padding and shaping measurably degrade it | Padding barely moves it |
| Expected AXON outcome | **BOUNDED** at stated overhead | **IMPOSSIBLE** at acceptable latency |

Reporting a padding scheme's benefit against WF as though it were a benefit
against correlation is the standard overclaim in this field, and §27.2's
pre-registration rule exists partly to prevent it here.

### 32.2 The base-rate discipline

WF results reported as closed-world accuracy are close to meaningless for a
deployed system. In an open world the quantity that matters is **precision at the
realistic prior**:

```text
  precision = TPR·p / ( TPR·p + FPR·(1−p) )

  p = 10⁻³ , TPR = 0.99 , FPR = 0.01  →  precision ≈ 0.090
  p = 10⁻³ , TPR = 0.95 , FPR = 0.001 →  precision ≈ 0.487
  p = 10⁻⁵ , TPR = 0.99 , FPR = 0.01  →  precision ≈ 0.001
```

A classifier with 99 % accuracy can be useless or decisive depending entirely on
the prior. **Every WF result this programme reports must state `p`, TPR, FPR and
precision.** Accuracy alone is not an acceptable report and a milestone that
produces only accuracy has not been met.

### 32.3 The AXON-specific finding: BULK traffic is free cover for INTERACTIVE

Cover traffic's problem everywhere it has been proposed is that it is pure waste:
bandwidth spent to carry nothing. **AXON is unusual in carrying two traffic
classes in one network, and one of them is bulk, continuous, latency-tolerant,
and doing real work** — erasure-coded shard transfer, repair, rebalancing, and
chain-evidence distribution (§31.2b), which is by itself ~2.7 GB/year per
participating node.

That suggests a mechanism that does not exist in Tor, I2P or Freenet because none
of them has both halves in the same network:

```text
   Conventional cover traffic:     pay bandwidth  →  get cover        (waste)
   AXON proposal:                  do storage work →  get cover free  (dual use)

   INTERACTIVE cells are multiplexed into circuits already carrying BULK
   shard traffic, at a shaped aggregate rate. The BULK flow is the padding,
   and it is padding that is simultaneously transferring real shards.
```

Properties to establish, and none of them is assumed:

1. **Does it actually help?** The BULK flow must be shaped so that adding
   interactive cells does not change the observable envelope. If it does, the
   cover is illusory and the mechanism is refuted.
2. **What does it cost the interactive stream?** Multiplexing into a shaped bulk
   flow adds latency and jitter. If it pushes interactive latency past usability
   the mechanism is refuted for that class.
3. **Does it leak the class anyway?** A relay carrying the merged flow may still
   distinguish. This is the primary experiment.
4. **Is it available?** A node doing no storage work has no cover. The mechanism
   is only as good as the node's participation, which makes it *incentive-linked*
   in a way the accounting plane can act on.

This is marked `[NEEDS RESEARCH]` and it is the most promising original idea in
the programme. It could also fail entirely on point 1.

### 32.4 The seventeen fields

| Field | Content |
|---|---|
| **Threat model** | Observes packet timing, size, direction, volume, duration, burst structure, circuit creation, and endpoint availability. WF adversary at one point; correlation adversary at both. Classifier-equipped, including modern deep-learning classifiers |
| **Current AXON weakness** | Fixed cells remove per-message length only. No padding machine, no shaping, no defended traffic class. R2 declares `INTERACTIVE` undefended and §16 defers everything meaningful |
| **Security objective** | **WF:** classifier precision below a pre-registered threshold at `p = 10⁻³`, at ≤ 50 % bandwidth overhead and ≤ 100 ms added median latency. **Correlation:** produce the measured curve and, if the expected result holds, state the impossibility explicitly rather than shipping a defence that does not work |
| **Candidate mechanisms** | Circuit-level padding machines with negotiated state machines; constant-rate shaping for `BULK`; adaptive/congestion-aware padding; the §32.3 dual-use cover; burst suppression; circuit scheduling; dummy circuits; delayed publication for the storage layer; traffic splitting across disjoint paths |
| **Mechanisms rejected** | **Constant-rate for `INTERACTIVE`** — the overhead and latency are incompatible with R2's class definition; it works, and it is not deployable. **"Add padding" without a state machine** — unmeasurable and historically ineffective. **Per-packet mixing for `INTERACTIVE`** — this is a mixnet, and R2 already ruled |
| **Protocol changes** | Padding-machine negotiation in the circuit handshake; a padding cell command already reserved in §8.1; class-aware scheduling at the relay |
| **Cryptographic changes** | None. Padding cells are indistinguishable from data cells by construction under §8.3's per-hop AEAD, which is a property worth stating explicitly here |
| **DHT changes** | None |
| **Economic changes** | Padding consumes relay bandwidth that the accounting plane would otherwise pay for; if §14 exists, padding must be compensated or relays will disable it. This is a real incentive conflict and it belongs in §33's calibration |
| **Implementation changes** | `tunnels/padding.go` (machines), `tunnels/schedule.go` (class-aware), plus a capture harness producing labelled traces |
| **Simulation methodology** | Packet-level simulation at small scale (10²–10³ nodes) — explicitly a *different* simulator from the Monte-Carlo path-selection model of §28, and §36 keeps them separate rather than pretending one tool does both |
| **Adversarial test methodology** | Evaluate against both statistical attacks and current deep-learning classifiers, in closed and open world, with the classifier **trained on defended traces** — evaluating a defence against a classifier trained on undefended traffic is the standard way to produce a fake result |
| **Metrics** | TPR, FPR, precision at stated `p`; mutual information between trace and destination; bandwidth overhead; added median and p99 latency; correlation TPR at fixed FPR for the two-ended adversary |
| **Milestones** | M5.1 trace capture harness and a labelled dataset from the local network. M5.2 baseline attack results on undefended AXON traffic. M5.3 padding machines implemented. M5.4 defended-trace evaluation with retrained classifiers. M5.5 §32.3 dual-use cover experiment. M5.6 correlation study and the explicit statement of its result |
| **Exit criteria** | E5.1 A baseline exists: attack performance against undefended AXON traffic, reported with precision at stated `p`. E5.2 A defence configuration meets the pre-registered WF threshold within the overhead budget — **falsified by the sweep, and failure here is an expected and acceptable outcome**. E5.3 The correlation result is published whatever it shows. E5.4 The §32.3 experiment returns a yes or a no, and a no is written into §40.4. E5.5 No defence is recommended on closed-world accuracy |
| **Residual risks** | End-to-end correlation. Endpoint availability patterns, which no padding hides. Application-layer behaviour above L8, entirely outside AXON's control |
| **New attacks introduced** | **Padding-machine fingerprinting** — the negotiated machine is itself a distinguisher, and a rare configuration identifies its user; machines must be few and defaults strong. **Class distinguishability** — `BULK` and `INTERACTIVE` are visibly different at a relay unless §32.3 works, so the traffic-class API of §20 may itself be a leak. **Padding as a DoS vector** — a client that negotiates expensive padding on many circuits consumes relay capacity for free |

### 32.5 What this workstream does NOT establish

- Protection against an adversary observing both ends. The expected deliverable
  is a measurement and a statement, not a defence.
- Protection above L8. Application behaviour is the dominant real-world leak and
  §18.21 already says so.
- That defended-trace results generalise. A classifier published after this work
  may defeat the defence, and WF results have a poor track record of aging well.
- Anything about the deployed network. Traces from a 100-node lab have no
  established relationship to a real population.

### 32.6 Comparison

| Source | Classification | What changes in AXON | Property that does not transfer |
|---|---|---|---|
| Tor — circuit padding framework / WTF-PAD lineage | `MODIFIED` | Adopted as the negotiation and machine model | Its calibration, which was done against Tor's traffic mix, not one containing continuous bulk storage traffic |
| Mixnets (Nym and the Loopix lineage) — Poisson mixing, loop cover | `REJECTED` for `INTERACTIVE`, `CANDIDATE` for `BULK` | Latency budget; R2's class split makes partial adoption coherent | Mixnet-grade unlinkability. Adopting the mechanism for `BULK` does not license the claim for anything else |
| Constant-rate defences (the BuFLO/Tamaraw lineage) | `REJECTED` as default, retained as the upper bound in the overhead study | They work; the cost is the problem | — |
| Freenet — bulk, latency-tolerant traffic | `NEW` in combination | §32.3's dual-use cover is only possible because AXON carries both classes | Freenet does not have a low-latency class to protect, so the idea has no analogue there |

## 33. Workstream 6 — Economic and Sybil Calibration

### 33.1 The finding: the weighting function decides everything, and it is a trilemma

Let an entity hold total stake `S` and split it across `k` identities. Under a
weighting function `w(·)` applied per identity, its total selection weight is
`k · w(S/k)`. The behaviour of that expression is not a detail:

| `w(s)` | `k·w(S/k)` vs `w(S)` | Effect on splitting | Effect on concentration |
|---|---|---|---|
| Concave, e.g. `√s` | `√(kS) > √S` — **increases with k** | **Rewards Sybils** | Resists plutocracy |
| Linear, `s` | `S` — **invariant** | Neutral | Neutral: weight ∝ capital |
| Convex, e.g. `s²` | `S²/k < S²` — **decreases with k** | Penalises Sybils | **Amplifies plutocracy** |

**The result, stated plainly: stake weighting alone cannot be simultaneously
Sybil-resistant and anti-plutocratic.** Concave weighting — the obvious choice
for limiting whale dominance, and the one quadratic-voting intuitions suggest —
actively pays an adversary to fragment into many identities, which is the exact
behaviour Sybil resistance is meant to prevent. This is a modelling result, not a
formal theorem, and it holds for any per-identity weighting; it is the reason
§15's "bonded stake" needs calibration before it can be called a defence.

**The escape is a per-identity fixed cost.** With a minimum bond `B_min`, an
entity can create at most `k ≤ S/B_min` identities, so concave weighting's
splitting reward is capped:

```text
   max weight  =  (S/B_min) · w(B_min)      for concave w
   choose B_min such that this is acceptable, and the design becomes:

       concave weighting          (limits whale dominance)
     + minimum bond floor B_min   (caps the splitting reward)
     + diversity constraints      (caps identities per /24 and per ASN)
     + lock period L > epoch      (defeats borrowed capital)
```

That combination is defensible. Each term without the others is not.

### 33.2 The cost formula

For selection weight linear in effective stake, with honest stake `S_h`, an
adversary seeking fraction `x` of selection probability must hold

```text
   S_a  =  x·S_h / (1 − x)

   x = 0.01 →  0.0101·S_h        x = 0.20 →  0.250·S_h
   x = 0.05 →  0.0526·S_h        x = 0.30 →  0.429·S_h
   x = 0.10 →  0.111·S_h
```

and the cost of holding it for `y` epochs with lock period `L`:

```text
   C(x,y)  =  S_a · r · (y+L)/E     opportunity cost at rate r, E epochs/year
            +  P_slash · S_a         expected slashing
            +  N_prefix · c_infra    diversity-constrained infrastructure
   where N_prefix ≥ (identities required) and c_infra is per-prefix/per-ASN cost
```

Two consequences the workstream must confront rather than report neutrally:

- **`C` is dominated by `S_h`.** Security is proportional to how much honest
  capital is locked, which is a quantity the protocol does not control and cannot
  predict. A network with little staked value is cheap to attack regardless of
  the mechanism's elegance.
- **`C` is an opportunity cost, not an expenditure.** An adversary who does not
  get slashed keeps the principal. The real price of a one-year 20 % attack is
  `0.25·S_h·r` — at `r = 5 %`, roughly **1.25 % of the honest stake**, recoverable
  in full. That is much cheaper than "you must acquire 25 % of the stake" makes
  it sound, and stating it this way is the workstream's most important output.

### 33.3 The seventeen fields

| Field | Content |
|---|---|
| **Threat model** | Large capital; many small identities; borrowed or flash capital; cartels of independent operators; compromised legitimate nodes; and an adversary optimising jointly across §33 and §35 (buy some capacity, fake the rest) |
| **Current AXON weakness** | §15's layered defence is uncalibrated and directionally unexamined; no `B_min`, no `L`, no weighting function, no `C(x,y)`. The interaction in §33.1 has never been checked |
| **Security objective** | `C(x = 0.20, y = 30 epochs)` computed and defended, with the derivation and the sensitivity to `S_h` published |
| **Candidate mechanisms** | Concave weighting + `B_min` + diversity caps + lock period `L`; capacity-bounded claims (§35); slashing on detected misbehaviour; identity age as a weight; randomised selection so an adversary cannot choose its position (§8.7) |
| **Mechanisms rejected** | **Pure proof-of-work admission** — pays a permanent energy cost for a one-time barrier and is trivially rented. **Unbounded delegation** — concentrates weight while distributing the appearance of it; if adopted at all it must be capped, and the cap is the mechanism. **Reputation without stake** — bootstraps from nothing, so a patient adversary simply waits |
| **Protocol changes** | Weighting function published as a network parameter (chain-anchored, per §22's upgrade mechanism); descriptor carries bond reference and lock expiry |
| **Cryptographic changes** | None |
| **DHT changes** | Bond references must be checkable without a chain call on the hot path — §7.9 already requires this and this workstream makes it load-bearing |
| **Economic changes** | This *is* the economic change: `B_min`, `L`, `w(·)`, slashing conditions, diversity caps, all calibrated jointly and all reusing `StakeVault` |
| **Implementation changes** | `accounting/weight.go`; selection integration in `routing/select.go`; bond verification cache |
| **Simulation methodology** | Adversary-optimisation model: given a budget, solve for the allocation across stake, identities, prefixes and faked capacity that maximises `x`. **The simulation must optimise on the adversary's behalf**, because evaluating a fixed naive strategy produces a flattering and useless number |
| **Adversarial test methodology** | Flash-capital attack across an epoch boundary; cartel formation; delegation concentration; joint optimisation with §35's measurement attack |
| **Metrics** | `C(x,y)` surface; sensitivity `∂C/∂S_h`; maximum `x` achievable at fixed budget; splitting gain under the chosen `w` |
| **Milestones** | M6.1 the §33.1 analysis reviewed and either confirmed or corrected. M6.2 parameter search over `(w, B_min, L, caps)`. M6.3 adversary optimiser. M6.4 `C(x,y)` published with sensitivity. M6.5 parameters proposed with the plutocracy statement attached |
| **Exit criteria** | E6.1 `C(0.20, 30)` is published as a formula in `S_h`, `r` and `c_infra`, with worked values at three plausible `S_h`. E6.2 The chosen `w` and `B_min` demonstrably cap splitting gain below a pre-registered factor. E6.3 A flash-capital adversary cannot acquire epoch weight — falsified by any successful cross-epoch attack. E6.4 The adversary optimiser finds no allocation beating the analytic bound by more than a pre-registered margin. E6.5 **The write-up states, in plain language, the degree to which the mechanism is pay-to-control** |
| **Residual risks** | Plutocracy is not eliminated, only priced. Security scales with honest stake, which the protocol cannot control. A wealthy adversary with no need to profit is unaffected by opportunity cost |
| **New attacks introduced** | **Bond-driven centralisation of high-value roles** — §28's layered guards require higher bonds, so the most security-critical positions are held by the wealthiest operators. **Slashing as an attack** — if slashing conditions are gameable, an adversary destroys honest operators' bonds. **Lock-period rigidity** — a long `L` deters honest participation more reliably than it deters a funded adversary |

### 33.4 What this workstream does NOT establish

- That AXON is Sybil-resistant. It establishes a price, and §40.4 records that a
  price is not the same thing.
- That the price is high enough. That depends on `S_h`, which is unknown and,
  for a new network, small.
- Anything about non-economic Sybil defence. The prefix and diversity terms of
  §15 are bounded by cloud-address economics, which this workstream measures but
  does not improve.
- That the concavity result is a theorem. It is a modelling argument and should
  be reviewed as one.
